The primary source of Si(OH)4 to the oceanic water column is from upwelling of deep-ocean Si(OH)4, which originates from remineralization of biogenic silica (bSiO2). Coastal zones also receive contributions from river input and groundwater discharge. In surface waters, Si(OH)4 is assimilated by siliceous phytoplankton, mostly diatoms. Biogenic silica dissolution occurs in both oxic and anoxic waters and in sediments. The activity of benthic macrofauna indirectly affects dissolution rates by changing the exposure of bSiO2 to varying levels of Si(OH)4- undersaturated seawater and/or sediment. In contrast to the N and P cycles, the Si cycle is not redox sensitive.Impacts of climate change on ocean deoxygenation and biogeochemical cyclesGlobal warming greatly impacts the physical and biogeochemical processes that drive the development of long-term hypoxia and ODZs in marine environments, including metabolic rates, stratification, ocean circulation, and winds30. Changing winds impact upwelling intensity and atmospheric deposition30. Changes in precipitation and flooding alter anthropogenic nutrient inputs, which may amplify climatic impact-drivers44,45. In turn, ocean deoxygenation, amplified by changes in O2 solubility and associated changes in redox conditions, affects community structure and biogeochemical cycles39,46,47. The impacts of climatic drivers affecting O2 and nutrient cycles in ODZs are reviewed below. Hydrocarbon oxidation has also been associated with O2 and nutrient depletion, but it is not further discussed in this review (e.g., in the Gulf of Mexico45,48).Decrease in oxygen solubility and stratificationIncreases in mean sea surface temperatures (0.6 °C between 1980 and 2020)30 and marine heatwaves reduce the solubility of O2 and hence its availability to organisms49,50. O2 solubility decreases non-linearly with increasing temperature, e.g., corresponding to a decrease of 2.5 micromoles of O2 per half a degree Celsius (at 15 °C and salinity of 35)51,52. Therefore, the greatest impacts would be expected to occur in high-latitude regions that ventilate the ocean interior. The ocean surface temperature is projected to increase further between 2018 and 2100 on average by 0.86 [0.43–1.47, likely range] °C according to the SSP1-2.6 model projection and by 2.89 [2.01 to 4.07, likely range] °C in SSP5-8.530. Overall, warming is estimated to account for about 15% of global ocean O2 loss, and more than 50% of the oxygen loss in the upper 1000 m of the ocean10,12,24,53.Warming of the surface ocean also decreases its density, thereby enhancing stratification. Greater stratification due to warmer temperatures is primarily observed at low latitudes. By decreasing mixing and ventilation of the ocean interior, increased stratification promotes ocean deoxygenation10,53,54,55. There is a consequence of stratification that needs to be considered: a decrease in nutrient supply to surface waters from the deep-sea reservoir56. A reduced supply of limiting nutrients can lower surface ocean productivity and the subsequent export of organic matter, thereby decreasing O2 demand in underlying waters. If ventilation rates remain unchanged, lowering productivity would lead to higher regional O2 concentrations57,58,59.Changes in community structure and biological respiration ratesThe increase in temperature and decrease in O2 levels are expected to alter the composition of microbial and phytoplankton communities. For instance, different O2 regimes were shown to modulate phytoplankton diversity in the coastal tropical Southeast Pacific ODZ. New production was dominated by large phytoplankton (diatoms) with low N:P ratios ( < 16:1) in the ODZ. On the other hand, smaller (pico/nano and micro) phytoplankton with intermediate N:P ratios close to Redfield or higher ( > 20:1) were prevalent in more oxygenated subsurface waters above the shelf break and offshore. Interestingly, excess phosphate liberated from the sediments under anoxic conditions did not stimulate N2 fixation60.The biochemical response of the microbial community to variations in O2 levels is intricate and difficult to predict. This complexity arises because aerobic and anaerobic microbial processes can often occur simultaneously, even in waters with low or possibly negligible O2 concentrations. In recent years, cryptic cycling of O2 and sulfur in the anoxic zone has been discovered61,62. The expression of the metabolic pathways involved in nitrogen cycling, such as nitrification, anammox, denitrification, and inorganic carbon fixation, is also linked to changes in O2 and the distribution patterns of common ODZ microbes, such as nitrifiers (Thermoproteota, (formerly Thaumarchaeota), Nitrospina, Nitrospira), anammox bacteria (Planctomycetes), and chemoautotrophic denitrifiers (e.g., the SUP05 group within the Gammaproteobacteria)63,64. For example, Thermoproteota with active nitrification and inorganic carbon fixation are predominant in low-oxic waters, while the SUP05 group of NO3--reducing sulfur oxidizers linked to active denitrification, sulfur oxidation, and inorganic carbon fixation are more prevalent in anoxic waters63. O2 is consumed during organic matter degradation, with the highest O2 utilization rates in the upper thermocline59,67. Two main factors influence respiration: the supply of organic matter and the rate of enzymatic metabolic processes involved. The specific effect of temperature on biological respiration processes is influenced by several factors (depth, light, nitrogen, iron, and carbon limitation) that are overall still not well understood45. Increases in respiration rates due to warming will also affect other metabolic rates and associated biogeochemical cycling, such as nutrient limitation for phytoplankton68 or O2 production69,70. Warming and higher respiration enhance NO3- regeneration and recycling in the euphotic zone, which increases primary productivity71. Higher primary production above ODZs may lead to increased export production and O2 consumption below the euphotic zone due to the degradation and respiration of organic matter, potentially expanding these ODZs. However, metabolic activity in ODZs has been shown to decrease at lower O2 concentrations and under nutrient limitation in the Eastern Tropical South Pacific72. Both a decrease in O2 (−5%) and an increase in nutrients (+0.5%), which are realistic under current climate change projections, could expand the hypoxic zone by 20–32%. Interestingly, the combined influence from these biogeochemical drivers greatly exceeded the effects of strengthening in upwelling-favorable winds (10% increase) and global warming (3% increase) alone44.Oceanic mesoscale circulation, including eddies, plays an important role in mixing heat, carbon, and nutrients. Satellite altimetry records have shown that mesoscale eddies have been increasing by 2–5% per decade in oceanic eddy-rich regions due to ongoing climate change80. Mesoscale activity is particularly enhanced in eastern boundary upwelling systems81,82,83,84,85. Eddies may inject nutrients into the euphotic zone, enhancing primary productivity, particularly in the open ocean. In contrast, models show that eddies could suppress coastal primary productivity by transporting nutrients from the nearshore environment to the open ocean, and counteracting wind-driven upwelling in eastern boundary upwelling systems86. In the Eastern Tropical South Pacific off Peru, transport of highly productive waters offshore by an anticyclonic mode water eddy and subsequent high organic matter respiration rates promoted denitrification and near complete NO3- exhaustion (i.e., high N loss) at the center of the eddy27,85,87. N2 fixation and carbon fixation rates were concurrently enhanced in the mode water eddies88. Open-ocean low-O2 zones (with [O2] as low as 2 μmol kg−1) were also found to develop within cyclonic and anticyclonic mode-water eddies during transport from the northwestern Africa coast in the Eastern Tropical North Atlantic89,90,91. In this region, enhanced nutrient supply to the euphotic zone in anticyclonic mode-water eddies was shown to greatly increase primary productivity92. Denitrification and enhanced N loss were also reported within these eddies93. Given the broad distribution of low-O2 eddies, these processes could be relevant to all eastern boundary upwelling systems94.Similarly, changes in fine-scale ocean currents could increase periodic O2 intrusions into ODZs, sustaining aerobic NOB. These intrusions allow aerobic NOB to grow and consume O2 at the ODZ boundaries. In turn, anoxia enables anaerobic bacteria to replenish NO2-, creating a cycle that maintains the anoxic environment. Thus, NOB could provide major stabilizing feedback to ODZs volume under climate change and affect greenhouse gas production (e.g., N2O)95.Changes in upwelling intensityGlobal warming is expected to increase the temperature difference between land and sea and cause stronger upwelling-favorable alongshore winds in coastal regions, particularly at high latitudes, with both meridional and seasonal shifts in upwelling strenght96,97,98,99. Change in upwelling intensity driven by global warming is projected to increase nutrient supply to sunlit surface waters, and subsequently, export organic matter resulting from enhanced primary production at the surface and O2 consumption from respiration in deeper waters45. In the North Pacific ODZ, a study observed a concomitant increase in NO3-, PO43-, and Si(OH)4 and a decrease in O2 associated with increased wind-driven circulation100, likely related to the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation101. Other possible causes for these changes include mesoscale eddies, the phase of El Niño, and seasonal changes98. In the coastal southern Benguela upwelling system, despite a projected increase in upwelling intensity, no clear long-term trend in O2 concentration is observed102. The projected increase in upwelling intensity could reduce the extent of nutrient trapping by increasing the offshore transport of particulate materials. Reduced nutrient trapping efficiency could thus, in part, counteract ODZ expansion due to changes in upwelling intensity102.Upwelling intensity is also influenced by El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a climate phenomenon characterized by the periodic warming (El Niño) and cooling (La Niña) of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. This cyclic event influences global weather patterns, leading to shifts in precipitation, temperature, and atmospheric circulation. As such, marine heatwaves are heavily linked to El Niño, which is often responsible for extreme ocean warming. ENSO is expected to become more intense and frequent with global warming103,104. ENSO affects oceanic nutrient cycling through changes in sea surface temperatures, altering the distribution of phytoplankton and zooplankton in the equatorial Pacific. During El Niño events, warmer sea surface temperatures suppress the upwelling of nutrient-rich cold waters, reducing primary productivity, respiration, and apparent O2 utilization (AOU)59,105. Denitrification rates were also reduced (up to 70% lower) during an El Niño event, with strong implications for the nitrogen budget106. La Niña is characterized by cooler sea surface temperatures, enhancing upwelling, nutrient supply, and primary productivity. Elevated primary production by phytoplankton during La Niña events supports higher zooplankton populations, thereby cascading through the entire marine ecosystem. Water column denitrification is strongly amplified during La Niña events, driven by shoaling of the upper boundary of the ODZ107. Yet, the changes in solubility and apparent O2 utilization during El Niño and La Niña overall compensate each other, weakening the magnitude of O2 variability59.Changes in atmospheric depositionAlterations in wind patterns due to global warming will also affect atmospheric deposition of nutrients, particularly in oligotrophic open-ocean regions. Atmospheric depositions of NOx and dissolved NH4+ have tripled since the industrial108. For instance, the South China Sea is subjected to particularly high anthropogenic depositions due to its proximity to densely populated areas. An increase in nutrient inputs from the atmosphere was observed in this region and was associated with greater biological production, O2 depletion, and carbon export109,110. In contrast, ocean warming, acidification, increased stratification, and associated food web changes are also expected to affect reactive nitrogen emissions from the ocean. Elevated biological process rates under a warmer climate may increase the production of ammonia (NH3) or organic nitrogen that could efflux to the atmosphere111. The release of volatile nitrogen compounds into the atmosphere can decrease the inventory of fixed nitrogen if they are deposited on land rather than returned to the ocean, lowering primary and export production. This process may consequently reduce respiration and shrink the geographical extent and thickness of ODZs.Nutrients, particularly Fe, are mainly deposited as dust in subtropical waters of the Northern Hemisphere, which are closest to desert regions112. Atmospheric inputs of iron and fixed nitrogen could, however, be transported from their region of deposition in the subtropics to the tropics113. Atmospheric depositions were also shown to support new production in upwelling regions114. Another biogeochemical model suggests that atmospheric iron inputs could support more than 25% of the net oceanic export production, with smaller contributions from N (5%), Si (0.2%), and P (0.1%)115. For instance, iron atmospheric inputs could greatly increase N2 fixation (especially in N-limited regions)116 and primary production, enhancing organic matter respiration deeper in the water column and ODZs expansion. Yet, a global ocean model indicated that the influence of atmospheric depositions on marine primary productivity was minimal. Specifically, while atmospheric depositions contributed to an increase in primary productivity, this effect was offset by net nitrogen loss due to denitrification occurring in ODZs117.Increases in precipitation, flooding, and nutrient inputs in coastal dead zones and ODZsClimate change affects marine and terrestrial processes, such as precipitation and flooding, altering anthropogenic nutrient inputs into coastal waters from rivers and coastal groundwater118,119. Nutrient inputs, from anthropogenic or natural sources, either by rivers, estuaries, and their tributaries, or from coastal groundwater discharge, can supply nutrients to nearshore marine regions, which further exacerbate eutrophication and the potential for O2 depletion, intensifying low-O2 environments24,45,120. The effects of climate change on nutrient inputs and cycling from riverine and groundwater discharges in coastal waters are further reviewed in a companion manuscript120.Positive feedback on global warming from greenhouse gas production in ODZsAtmospheric warming is further enhanced due to the liberation of greenhouse gases, such as CH4 and N2O, that are naturally produced under low-O2 or anoxic conditions in ODZs and marine dead zones121,122,123. Thus, while nutrient inputs from atmospheric deposition, riverine inputs, and coastal groundwater discharge can enhance primary production and hence potentially act to increase carbon sinks, they can also stimulate the production of the potent greenhouse gas N2O, which is enhanced by low-O2 conditions124. N2O is 270 times more potent than CO2 on a per-molecule basis and is the main ozone-depleting substance in the stratosphere125,126. Coastal upwelling systems associated with ODZs account for up to 35 % of total oceanic N2O emissions35,125,127,128, but it is uncertain how these fluxes might change in the future. The development of anoxic conditions in dead zones or in the cores of ODZs also favors the production of the greenhouse gas CH4, which predominantly occurs in shallow near-shore environments. CH4 is 27 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than CO2 on a per molecule basis125. However, while CH4 accumulates at relatively high levels in the anoxic cores of ODZs (20–105 nM)129, it is rapidly re-oxidized to CO2 in oxic waters. Consequently, total marine CH4 emissions (6–12 Tg yr−1) account only for up to ~6% of all natural emissions130. Production of these greenhouse gases, caused by lower O2 conditions in ODZs, further enhances warming, which positively impacts ocean deoxygenation (Fig. 1). However, a decrease in net primary productivity and export resulting from increased stratification, especially in low to mid latitudes, may lead to a reduction in the release of these greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, since they are emitted as a byproduct of remineralization131.Fig. 1: Effects of climatic impact-drivers on nutrient cycling (P, N, Si) in marine ODZs.Full size imageGlobal warming reduces gas solubility and increases stratification in the surface ocean (1, 2) but increases respiration and metabolic rates (including primary production rates and the amount of organic matter exported) (3), and impacts ocean circulation (4). Increase in alongshore winds impacts coastal upwelling intensity (5) and atmospheric deposition (6). Changes in precipitation impact the delivery of nutrients from rivers and groundwater discharge (7). Nutrient inputs from atmospheric depositions, riverine inputs, and coastal groundwater discharges stimulate the production of greenhouse gases and their emission to the atmosphere (8).The alternating phases of ENSO also drive large variability in N2O emissions106,107. Specifically, net N2O production is highly sensitive to oxygenation and changes in ODZ volume106,107. Thus, the response of N2O to climate variability might be even stronger than the response of denitrification, which could lead to larger production pulses during La Niña and minimum production during El Niño episodes106,107. Recent studies highlight that, under certain circumstances (i.e., high OM availability), NO3--denitrifying bacteria can extend N2O production into more oxygenated waters, making them a major contributor to N2O emissions in ODZs, an important finding for predicting future N2O emissions132,133.Another example is the northern Indian Ocean, where N2O production along ODZs and emissions to the atmosphere are spatially decoupled, with the majority of the N2O emitted in regions of coastal upwelling, winter convection, or turbulent mixing134. This finding highlights the important role of ocean circulation, which, along with environmental factors, controls ocean circulation that modulates N2O emissions135.N2O accumulation and emission from the ocean are sensitive to climate variability, but it is unclear if ongoing ODZs expansion will overall lead to increased fluxes of N2O and CH4 to the atmosphere. Further study is needed to examine these potential feedbacks.Socio-economic impactsProjected increases in ocean deoxygenation, the areal extent of ODZs, and changes in nutrient cycling are expected to have socio-economic impacts. Yet, the socio-economic consequences of climate change on ODZs, nutrient cycles, and marine life remain speculative due to the scarcity of statistically robust studies directly linking anthropogenic climate change to negative outcomes in ODZs and dead zones. Coastal areas provide essential ecosystem services, such as recreational activities, fisheries, transport, and energy production. The expansion of marine ODZs reduces the volume of oxic shallow waters where most human interaction with the ocean occurs and where many nutritionally and economically important species thrive. Certain microorganisms and marine animals that cannot carry out photosynthesis rely on aerobic metabolism. Minor fluctuations in O2 and nutrient levels can thus greatly affect marine ecosystems, along with associated services and functions136,137,138,139. Coastal regions, characterized by reduced ventilation and increased primary productivity, are particularly susceptible to deoxygenation. This vulnerability is exacerbated by multiple stressors, such as river influences, runoff, land use changes, and anthropogenic disturbances.Changes in O2 and nutrient levels within and surrounding ODZs and dead zones also impact fisheries and the livelihoods of human communities dependent on marine resources. Fish and shellfish industries will particularly be affected as fish are the most sensitive to hypoxia, followed by crustaceans, echinoderms, annelids, and mollusks6. However, it is important to emphasize that the taxonomic level of an organism typically provides restricted insights into the physiological effects of O2. For example, a study highlights species-specific variations instead of differences at higher taxonomic levels5. Organisms that are unable to move or possess restricted mobility, such as demersal fish, will be particularly impacted, along with benthic animals. Studies show that fish growth was impaired at O2 concentrations between 188 and 141 µmol kg−1 O2, while other aspects of aerobic metabolism are affected between 125 and 63 µmol kg−1 O26. However, even higher O2 thresholds have sublethal effects on animal behavior, ecological fitness, and geographic range, especially when the interactions with other climatic impact-drivers are considered (i.e., increase in temperature)5,139,140. Apart from supporting global food security, fish and shellfish provide many other ecosystem services, including supporting nutrient recycling in several marine habitats (e.g., coral reefs)141,142. The effects of global warming on fisheries systems also call for environmental and social justice considerations, as many impoverished and indigenous coastal communities depend on subsistence fishing. Climate impacts threaten their income, food security, and cultural heritage143,144,145.Research gaps and future research prioritiesClimate change is expected to accelerate ocean deoxygenation due to a continuous increase in temperature and impacts of other climatic-impact drivers, such as an intensification of alongshore winds and atmospheric depositions45. In turn, ODZ expansion could alter nutrient availability, thereby influencing global productivity, carbon sequestration, and greenhouse gas emissions. This review highlighted that physical and biogeochemical factors driving ocean deoxygenation and nutrient cycles are interlinked in complex ways, often synergistically, making it difficult to disentangle the impacts from individual climatic change drivers and nutrients. Also, the effects of warming and deoxygenation can be non-linear, leading to increases in metabolic rates as O2 concentrations decline to a threshold, beyond which metabolic rates decrease146. Future research priorities to better understand the impacts of climate change on nutrient cycling in ODZs include improved 1) experimental and mesocosm studies, 2) microbial and genomic investigations, 3) biogeochemical modeling, and 4) high spatial and temporal resolution observations.First, more experimental and mesocosm studies are needed to isolate the effects of temperature, carbon dioxide, and deoxygenation on nutrient cycling in ODZs. For instance, it is unclear how ODZ expansion will affect nutrient regeneration versus loss by denitrification and/or anammox. The impacts of low O2 on nutrient stoichiometry (N:P:Fe ratios) and consequences for phytoplankton communities also need further investigation. Mesocosm experiments simulating future climate conditions in ODZ-like environments could help better understand the responses in nutrient cycling under isolated or multiple stressor conditions, such as warming, acidification, and deoxygenation. The feedback between ocean deoxygenation and atmospheric greenhouse gas fluxes (e.g., N2O) also requires further investigation.Second, a better understanding of the responses of microbial communities and marine organisms to warming, acidification, and deoxygenation is needed2. Several areas where more focused research is necessary include 1) investigating how the structure and function of microbial communities and higher trophic levels shift with changing O2 and nutrient regimes, 2) linking microbial diversity with nitrogen transformation pathways in ODZs using metagenomics and transcriptomics, and 3) studying how the antagonistic or symbiotic interactions (i.e., cooperation or competition) between microorganisms change under deoxygenation and warming.Third, current models often lack the resolution and complexity needed to simulate the interactions between climate-driven changes (e.g., temperature, stratification) and nutrient cycling in ODZs. A better representation of microbial metabolic diversity and its impact on nutrient (e.g., nitrogen, phosphorus, silicon) cycling needs to be incorporated into Earth system models147,148. The partitioning between denitrification, anammox, and nitrification under low-O2 conditions is also not well resolved, especially under in situ pressure conditions. Additionally, resolving future changes in atmospheric circulation, terrestrial runoff, and ocean circulation patterns and mesoscale features, such as eddies, will greatly improve biogeochemical models. Meso and sub-mesoscale processes, such as eddies, greatly influence ODZ biogeochemistry27,85,86,87,149,150. Socio-ecological models should also be used to evaluate the vulnerability of coastal communities to ODZ-induced changes in nutrient dynamics. This will allow the development of early warning systems and adaptation strategies for ecosystems dependent on coastal upwelling systems associated with ODZs for fisheries.Fourth, the lack of high-resolution observations and long-term observational datasets is a major gap in understanding current and future impacts of climatic drivers on nutrient dynamics and fluxes in ODZs and detecting trends. Higher spatial and temporal resolution could be achieved by deploying autonomous sensors (e.g., floats, gliders, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs)) and establishing sustained time series stations in ODZs. For instance, interpretation of highly resolved O2 and nutrient data obtained from the Biogeochemical Argo (or BGC-Argo) program will help improve understanding of the causes of O2 depletion and associated changes in nutrient cycles in ODZ151,152,153. One recent advance is the capability to detect NO2- at high spatiotemporal resolution using BGC-Argo floats154,155. In the future, efforts should focus on developing ocean nutrient sensors, such as PO43-, that can be deployed on autonomous platforms. Satellite data could also be used to improve long-term and spatially resolved estimates of surface productivity and nutrient limitation in ODZs.In summary, future research should use interdisciplinary methods combining field observations, including both discrete and high-resolution datasets from sensors on autonomous platforms or satellites, laboratory experiments, and earth system modeling. Shifts in nutrient dynamics can alter fisheries, food security, biodiversity, and ecosystem services. Yet, many unknowns remain, for instance, the effect of ODZs or dead zones on Si cycling is still not well understood. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the drivers and patterns of deoxygenation and the effects of deoxygenation on biogeochemical processes will help better predict future ocean productivity, manage marine resources, and mitigate climate feedback.

Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria: lingering household impacts, vulnerabilities, and resilience
                    Nilima Islam Luba1, Pallab Mozumder2, Sisi Meng3 & …Nafisa Halim4 Show authors

npj Environmental Social Sciences

volume 1,  Article number: 11 (2026) Cite this article
                    
                    
                        
                            
    
        
            
            
                
            Save article
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

Subjects
        
            Climate-change impactsEnvironmental studiesNatural hazardsSocioeconomic scenarios

AbstractThe year 2017 marked one of the most catastrophic U.S. hurricane seasons, encompassing three devastating hurricanes—Harvey, Irma, and Maria. Even three years after Hurricane Maria, 40% of Puerto Rican households still reported high or extreme impacts, reflecting a significant reduction in household well-being. This study evaluated the prolonged impacts of the hurricane by analyzing survey data from 502 Puerto Rican households, combined with GIS-based spatial factors. Findings reveal that extended utility disruptions, severe property damage, prolonged displacement, and income loss increased household impacts, while insufficient disaster aid further exacerbated them. However, proactive preparedness measures, e.g., alternative electricity sources to counter service interruptions, structural modifications to prevent damage, and insurance to mitigate financial burdens, significantly reduced the likelihood of severe impacts and promoted household resilience. While larger households displayed greater resilience, those with elderly members endured more adverse effects. These critical insights highlight the need for stronger and collaborative disaster management strategies and resilient infrastructure development to protect vulnerable regions against household impacts in future disasters.

IntroductionAnthropogenic climate change, coupled with the expanding coastal population, has amplified the effects of cyclone exposure globally1,2,3,4. Annually, tropical cyclones result in numerous fatalities, injuries, physical damage to property and infrastructure, livelihood and utility service disruptions, and population displacement. Research shows that the multifaceted consequences of hurricanes significantly affected household well-being5,6,7. The complexity of hazard events across locations leaves gaps in understanding how vulnerabilities and immediate hazard outcomes affect well-being and household resilience. Studying the households affected by Hurricane Maria, this research contributes to the literature on how major hurricanes shape long-term household well-being in vulnerable regions. This research answers the following:
                
                  How does hazard exposure contribute to prolonged household impact through utility disruptions, property damage, and temporary displacement?
                  We hypothesize that households with greater hazard exposure face significantly higher long-term impacts. Wind and flood exposure, utility disruptions, property damage, and temporary displacement are used as measures of exposure.
                
                
                  How do resilience mechanisms (e.g., proactive preparedness measures, disaster response) influence the extent of household impact in the long run?
                  We hypothesize that proactive preparedness measures, such as owning alternative electricity sources and having insurance, mitigate long-term impact and contribute to greater resilience.
                
              In disaster research, household well-being is typically defined as the overall physical, economic, and social condition of households before, during, and after a hazard event. Resilience is commonly understood as the capacity of households to withstand, adapt to, or recover from disaster impacts, often reflected in maintaining well-being despite exposure to hazards. Traditionally, well-being and resilience are measured using a combination of objective indicators (e.g., income loss, property damage, displacement) and subjective assessments (e.g., self-reported quality of life, perceived recovery)8,9,10,11,12.Figure 1 presents the conceptual framework. In the context of this study, we measure household well-being using Likert-scale self-reported household impact from a survey conducted three years after Hurricane Maria. This subjective measure reflects both the direct impacts experienced at the time of the hurricane and the lingering effects that persist up to the time of the survey. As time passes, respondents’ subjective ratings naturally integrate their initial exposure with their current circumstances. For example, households still affected by the hurricane are expected to report a higher impact level, reflecting both past and ongoing consequences. Under this framework, any reported impact indicates a reduction in household well-being, with higher scores reflecting greater declines and vulnerabilities, while households reporting no or minor impacts are considered resilient. We model objective indicators, including hurricane exposure, vulnerability (e.g., damage, utility disruptions, displacement), resilience mechanisms, disaster aid, and socio-economic household characteristics, as predictors of the self-reported impact. Addressing these challenges requires equitable actions to enhance disaster resilience in Puerto Rico.DiscussionThis study shows that severe damage and prolonged utility disruptions were the primary drivers of long-term household impact in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria. While protective measures like generators and insurance alleviate household impacts, disaster relief efforts failed to accelerate recovery. These findings emphasize the need for resilient infrastructure, protective actions, and more effective disaster management strategies.Energy, communication, and health infrastructure in Puerto Rico took the strongest blow from Hurricane Maria, which had a magnified effect at the household level. Our findings indicate that prolonged power, internet, cellphone, and public transportation disruptions were critical drivers of persistent impacts. Considering the multidimensional and complex effects of utility-service disruption, their implications need to be interpreted cautiously.Prolonged power failures cascaded across lifelines. Limited generator availability and fuel supplies constrained temporary cellular network and internet restoration efforts, and slowed full recovery36. In addition to sustained damage, power and network outages shut down the Tren Urbano and left many traffic signals inoperable30. As water pumping and treatment processes rely on electricity, water service disruption intensified47. Such disruptions forced many households to relocate48. Damaged roads and transit outages disrupted the supply chain, delaying repairs and services49,50. These compounding effects contributed to industry shutdowns, business closures, job losses, and additional displacement. Our results showed longer transportation disruption and more days of simultaneous power-internet outages associated with higher extent of household impact. The 2019 ASCE report card indicates poor conditions of the infrastructure post-restoration in hurricane Maria-affected communities51. The persistent impact after 3 years reflects the downstream consequences rather than the outage period alone. Non-significant association of water outage with household impact can be explained by temporary substitute supplies and more uniform restoration compared to other utilities.Given the interdependence of utility services and heavy reliance on electricity, strengthening the energy infrastructure is crucial. Despite the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) $3.2 billion allocation, a notable improvement in energy infrastructures was not observed in the following years51,52. Privatization of the power sector has led to increased charges and persistent grid instability53,54.Puerto Rico’s high susceptibility to sea-level rise further complicates efforts to reduce hazard exposure on infrastructure55. In 2022, Hurricane Fiona caused a complete power outage in Puerto Rico once again, underscoring the necessity of reliable alternative power sources56. Our results indicate alternative power sources like solar panels and generators can mitigate long-term hardships from power outages. Even severely damaged households with generators were in a better position to counter the adverse long-term effects compared to such households without a generator.The higher effectiveness of generators than solar panels at battling the adverse effects is likely due to existing housing practices in Puerto Rico. Prevalent informal construction practices and lack of maintenance in the region compromise the structural integrity required for secure solar panel installation57. Hurricane Maria’s strong winds caused extensive roof damage, rendering many solar panels nonfunctional.Current community solar grids may alleviate the inefficiency of traditional energy distribution systems to some extent. Reinforcing construction standards and integrating micro-grid solutions could enhance the benefits from solar panels as a sustainable alternative power source. However, ensuring generator availability and emergency fuel reserves remain essential for the foreseeable future.This study shows that older houses experienced higher impacts, which is potentially due to construction malpractice. Informal inheritance, unregulated construction, and reconstruction violations-often linked to limited financial resources and lack of awareness- led to the rejection of many federal relief claims58,59,60. This lack of access to federal relief can explain the insignificance of aid in lessening impacts and widespread household dissatisfaction with federal government assistance.FEMA categorized Hurricane Maria property damage as moderate damage <$17,000, major damage: >=$17,000, and destroyed (not economically feasible to repair, for planning and communication purposes61. However, it relies on Safe, Sanitary, and Functional (SSF) standards to determine individual assistance eligibility for “essential repairs”. Such approaches fail to capture the wide variation in household damage and overlook renter-specific impacts. FEMA’s “insufficient damage” label disproportionately excludes the lowest-income households from receiving assistance. The US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) later developed separate standardized dollar/flood depth categories for Community Development Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR). The CDBG-DR “unmet-need” categorization was more inclusive of renter impacts and meeting their needs62. In line with previous literature, our study found that renter-occupied houses faced major damage, while their income declined more than the owners’63.Instead of SSF’s absolute loss thresholds, the FEMA individual assistance eligibility should also use the damage-to-income metric and be more inclusive of renters. This study shows that modifying homes for storm-proofing significantly improved household well-being. This reinforces the need for government support in renovating older, vulnerable structures. However, informal housing practices complicate insurance eligibility. Lack of property title was the primary cause of FEMA application denials and also caused insurance enrollment ineligibility. Both Federal assistance and insurance eligibility criteria need to be adjusted to accommodate such homeowners.Our study determined that uninsured households were significantly more susceptible to hurricane impacts. Lack of insurance further increases the vulnerability of informal housing and widens the gap between damage incurred and insurance coverage. This study highlights lower flood insurance enrollment and flood awareness among Puerto Rican households. Many lack awareness about coverage specifics, including the exclusion of flood damage. Many of the flooded households in this study were located outside the designated flood zones, yet suffered flood damage. Considering such flooding instances, the flood zone delegation in Puerto Rico needs to be updated. Given Puerto Rico’s climate vulnerability, expanding flood insurance awareness and accessibility regardless of home location is essential to strengthen household resilience.Puerto Rico’s territorial status and colonial governance practices notably constrained household recovery. Though the island’s economy was in decline, as a U.S. territory, it was ineligible for most forms of international financial assistance. Fiscal autonomy of Puerto Rico has further narrowed since Congress’s enactment of the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA) in 2016. It installed an unelected Fiscal Oversight and Management Board that demoted social investment and prioritized debt services64. Compared to other major hurricane-affected regions in 2017, Puerto Ricans faced discrimination in every aspect of federal response, from emergency personnel deployment to disaster relief distribution28. Our findings show that disaster aid had no significant impact, suggesting delays, insufficient quantity, unequal distribution, and logistical barriers hindering aid mechanisms28,43. Post-Maria infrastructural privatizations illustrate colonial governance instilling fragility into essential services.Puerto Rico’s reliance on mainland U.S. resources, combined with its physical distance and geopolitical differences, heightens vulnerability. The St. Jones Act restrictions increase domestic shipping cost and time, notably rising commodity prices on the island compared to the continental US65,66,67,68. In emergencies, Puerto Rico is able to receive limited external physical support because of the Act restricting foreign vessel use between domestic ports69. Eight days after Hurricane Maria, the Act was waived for 10 days only70. While the bureaucratic process to enact the waiver delayed disaster response, such short waiver duration was not deemed enough to aid the recovery process. We recommend establishing pre-defined criteria for automatic waivers to expedite disaster response in Puerto Rico and other non-continental US parts. Calibrating waiver length to real logistic timelines would alleviate bottlenecks and accelerate recovery.Agreement on Disaster Management and Emergency Response serves as a framework for disaster management cooperation between countries with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations71. Though the treaty has been around since 2009, more progressive efforts in disaster management can be observed in recent times. Developing a multinational structure in the Caribbean for collaborative disaster management can be highly beneficial to ensure secure and timely disaster management practices in Puerto Rico and the Caribbean islands.Our findings indicate the importance of a decentralized, locally driven, and proactive disaster management approach. This study reveals that extended energy, communication, and transportation interruptions directly affected the quality of life in Puerto Rico. Months of public transportation disruption constrained daily commute and access to essential services. Communication and transportation failures limited the scope of community-based recovery interventions, blocked household access to resources. Disruptions also halted supply chains—causing delays in utility and service restorations. The failure of the communication infrastructure accentuated the coordination gap between the federal and local governments, leading to an ineffective disaster response. Days before Maria, emergency supplies in Puerto Rican warehouses were sent to the U.S. Virgin Islands for Hurricane Irma response72. No immediate action had been taken to restock the Puerto Rican inventory. Lack of hurricane supplies in emergency warehouses and FEMA’s untimely and haphazard execution of relief distribution implicates ineffective top-down emergency planning and inadequate preparedness. Looking at the immediate response timeline for Hurricane Maria, we consider maintaining a constant stock of 1 week of emergency aid crucial until external disaster relief can arrive.Hurricane Maria caused permanent displacement and shutdown of numerous businesses, leading to household income and employment losses, as reflected in our findings25. The post-Maria poverty rate in Puerto Rico was projected to exceed 50%73. Even property values depreciated in communities near the hurricane path74. This study found relatively high expenses of hurricane supplies and temporary displacement, possibly amplifying the long-term financial constraints. Though financial indicators are widely used as reliable predictors of well-being, we found that direct monetary values are weak predictors of long-term subjective well-being.Elderly Puerto Ricans disproportionally suffered from the hurricane, and discriminatory assistance policies mostly undermined their needs75,76. While FEMA ran its longest-ever post-disaster meal program, the food was criticized for not meeting the federal nutritional guidelines77. Food insecurity increased for both elderly and younger adults after the hurricane and persisted in the following years78,79. Additional support is required for households with elderly members. Only 0.1% of the affected households received the maximum federal grant ($30,000) for Hurricane Maria-inflicted damage73.Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) and Community-Based Organizations (CBOs) were proactive compared to the government actors80,81. Different NGOs served meals and distributed food supplies among millions of Maria survivors for almost a year82,83,84. Other assistance included backup power/charging, drinking water, and water purification kit distribution, organizing debris removal, and coordinating medical supply and mental health services, etc.85,86. NGOs and tech organizations also collaborated to provide internet connections36,37. These organizations mobilized through local networks (e.g., community centers, faith-based organizations, neighborhood associations). While FEMA denied assistance to damaged households with informal practices (e.g., no property title), empirical evidence shows that NGOs stepped in to rebuild their houses. Rebuilding efforts provided opportunities to use new, wind-resistant materials to replace older structures, which in turn helped communities feel better prepared and more resilient for future hurricanes87. Decentralization and inter-agency collaboration, along with involving smaller non-profits operating at the grassroots level, can play a crucial role in accelerating Puerto Rico’s recovery80,88. While resilient infrastructure development is essential for economic progress, revising block fund-based assistance programs and income tax credit criteria can help expedite financial recovery through income smoothing73,89,90.While Hurricane Maria had a catastrophic impact in Puerto Rico, this study demonstrates that the region’s long-lasting extensive impacts from the event were fueled by its existing vulnerabilities, inadequate precaution, and incompetent disaster management practices73,91. We uniquely pair subjective survey measures in GIS-based spatial context and show how household protections shape impact. Our study provides a novel, comprehensive evaluation of Hurricane Maria’s long-term impacts on household well-being through damage, disruptions, and displacement.However, this study relies on self-reported measures of household well-being and other factors 3 years after the hurricane. Therefore, recall bias may cause over-/underestimation of impact severity, disruption lengths, income changes, related expenses, and so on. Between 2017 and 2020, parts of Puerto Rico were affected by a series of earthquakes (2019–2020), followed by the universal COVID-19 pandemic. These events affected the households before they could recover from Hurricane Maria. However, Puerto Rico’s Economic Activity Index had a much larger decline after Hurricane Maria than the later events92,93. Given the cross-sectional nature of the impact variable, we could not isolate the effect of these events on long-term hurricane impact perception of the households. In similar situations, future studies can collect impact and related data in a longitudinal manner, addressing each event. A small section of literature studies the non-health concerns in Puerto Rico during the early pandemic days in conjunction with Hurricane Maria. Finally, inequalities in finances were not deeply investigated in this research. Mixed-method follow-ups with individual groups (e.g., elderly, renters) can clarify mechanisms behind prolonged impact. Despite the limitations, our research depicts sustainable protective measures and offers adaptive solutions for disaster resilience in Puerto Rico. Policy recommendations derived from this study can be replicated to enhance disaster resilience in similar vulnerable regions.MethodsData collectionTo assess the self-reported impact of Hurricane Maria on long-term household well-being, we conducted a web-based survey using the Qualtrics platform and a quota sampling method between June and November 2020, almost three years after Hurricane Maria. The survey design followed the existing literature on natural hazards and subjective well-being5,71,94,95. The survey targeted Puerto Rico residents aged 18 and older who were impacted by Hurricane Maria. A total of 1782 adults initiated the survey, 1222 met the residency and home-at-landfall screening criteria, and 504 complete responses were retained for analysis. The sample spans 119 ZIP codes and covers most counties across the island, with a larger share from San Juan, indicating broad geographic coverage and representativeness. Though Qualtrics did their best to make sure the sample is representative of affected communities, respondents include a slightly higher share of younger adults and women, and have higher educational attainment than the general population, patterns consistent with online survey administration. Accordingly, we acknowledge that while our sample is broadly representative in geographic coverage and captures a wide cross-section of adult residents, it shows under coverage of men and lower-education groups.The survey covered household demographics, hurricane experience, incurred damage, utility-service disruptions, protective measures, aid and assistance, and self-reported impact levels. In the key survey question, respondents were asked to report the impact level of Hurricane Maria on their households on a Likert scale (1= No Impact, 2= Low Impact, 3= Some Impact, 4= High Impact, 5= Extreme Impact). The variables used in the analysis, along with their descriptions and summary statistics, are presented in Table 1. Notable characteristics include an average total property damage of $6466, 16% of respondents residing in flood zones, 58% lacking natural-hazard-related insurance at the time of the hurricane, and 45% receiving aid or assistance. Additionally, 19% of households owned a generator. The mean monthly income was $424, the average household size was 3.49, and 29% of households reported having an elderly member.To enhance geo-spatial analysis, supplementary spatial data were collected. Using hurricane tracts (best track) by NHC-NOAA in ArcGIS, we determine proximity to the hurricane path96. IBTrACS (International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship) data interpolation was used to determine maximum wind exposure at household locations97,98. This spatial data helps clarify variations in impact based on location-specific exposure levels. Tiger/line shapefiles from the US Census Bureau and USPS 5-digit zip-codes to define the administrative boundaries99. Income groups were determined by comparing household income with the US Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) income limit 2018 schedule for Puerto Rico100.Data analysisTo examine the determinants of long-term household impacts, we employed the Ordered Logit Regression model, which is suitable for analyzing ordinal dependent variables. Assuming homogeneity within and heterogeneity across zip-codes, we estimated the models at the zip-code level101. We reported seven regression specifications with diverse combinations of explanatory variables. This approach allowed us to examine how various factors uniquely influenced household impact. Odds ratios from these models are reported in Table 2.Furthermore, we estimated the marginal effects of the explanatory variables on household impact levels to illustrate the difference between vulnerable and resilient households. Marginal effects for “extreme impact” (Impact = 5) and “low impact” (Impact = 2) are reported in Table 3 and Table 4, respectively. The regression models revealed significant associations between hurricane exposure, utility disruptions, and household characteristics. To illustrate the variation in impact levels, we calculated the predictive margins for the continuous explanatory variables at distinct values. For categorical variables, we calculated the predictive margins at the corresponding categories. Plots of the predictive margins for total damage, evacuation duration, and alternative power sources are reported in Figs. 3–5.Finally, we presented two more specific marginal analyses in Table 5, based on the observed variation in the probability of predictive margins for the outcome levels. In the first analysis, we determined the contrast in predictive margins for generators (with generator vs. without) across four damage levels: $6466, $18,943, $31,419, and $43,896. This provided insight into the effectiveness of generators in mitigating household vulnerability and sustaining well-being, especially as damage severity levels increased.For the second analysis, we calculated the predictive margins for the Elderly at “Have Elderly Member/s” vs. “No Elderly Member” for Household sizes 1–12. This analysis highlighted how larger and smaller households with elderly members experience different levels of impact. Together, these insights can guide disaster preparedness and recovery efforts aimed at strengthening resilience for vulnerable populations.

items.title: MartinoRossi accelera sulla sostenibilità con il nuovo bilancio 2025 e il piano 2030
items.description: MartinoRossi spa, azienda cremonese specializzata in farine, ingredienti funzionali, prodotti plant-based e proteici da cereali e legumi senza glutine
items.body:
Sostenibilità

MartinoRossi accelera sulla sostenibilità con il nuovo bilancio 2025 e il piano 2030

Redazione

-

25 Luglio 2026

Un tecnico in campo verifica irrigazione e colture, simbolo di filiera controllata e sostenibilità nel settore agroalimentare.

MartinoRossi spa, azienda cremonese specializzata in farine, ingredienti funzionali, prodotti plant-based e proteici da cereali e legumi senza glutine, ha pubblicato nel 2026 il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 a Malagnino, in provincia di Cremona, per rendicontare i risultati ambientali, industriali e sociali raggiunti nell’ultimo anno e fissare nuovi obiettivi al 2030. Il documento, diffuso dall’azienda, registra la crescita delle materie prime da filiera controllata a 108.858 tonnellate (+26% sul 2024), la riduzione dei contratti in somministrazione del 68% e il rafforzamento del percorso interno certificato Great Place to Work.
MartinoRossi adotta il nuovo standard Vsme per il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025
La novità principale del Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 è l’adozione del nuovo standard volontario Vsme, Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard, ispirato ai principi degli Esrs e all’approccio della doppia materialità. Una scelta, spiega l’azienda, pensata per anticipare le evoluzioni normative europee e rendere più leggibili le informazioni rivolte a clienti, fornitori, comunità locali e altri stakeholder. Non un passaggio solo tecnico, dunque. Anche perché nel documento viene formalizzato il primo Piano di Sostenibilità 2026-2030, con obiettivi, target e indicatori su cambiamento climatico, risorse idriche, forza lavoro propria e condotta d’impresa.
“Il Bilancio di Sostenibilità rappresenta, anno dopo anno, non solo uno strumento di rendicontazione, ma anche l’espressione concreta del nostro modo di fare impresa”, ha detto Stefano Rossi, amministratore delegato di MartinoRossi. L’ad ha parlato di una gestione “responsabile, trasparente e orientata al lungo periodo”, aggiungendo che la sostenibilità per il gruppo “non rappresenta un semplice adempimento, ma un modello di gestione che orienta ogni decisione strategica”. Parole misurate, dentro una traiettoria già tracciata. E ora messa nero su bianco.
Agrifuture e Underdrip, la ricerca nei campi di Malagnino
Uno dei capitoli centrali riguarda Agrifuture, l’azienda agricola sperimentale avviata nel 2022 su 33 ettari di proprietà accanto allo stabilimento di Malagnino. È qui che agronomi e ricercatori lavorano, in collaborazione con università e clienti, su produzione agricola sostenibile, nuove varietà, ibridi più adatti ai processi aziendali, precision farming, biostimolanti e consociazione delle colture. Un laboratorio all’aperto, con parcelle osservate stagione dopo stagione. Non una vetrina, ma un campo di prova.Leggi ancheSono le mete ideali per chi lavora in smartworking: qui con 500€ al mese puoi vivere una vita nel lusso più sfrenatoBonus, fino al 50% di sconto se acquisti il tuo elettrodomestico dei sogni: controlla i requisiti e richiedilo subito
Tra i progetti testati in Agrifuture c’è Underdrip, tecnologia nata da un’idea del presidente Giorgio Rossi e sviluppata con l’Università degli Studi di Milano. Il sistema brevettato di subirrigazione di precisione distribuisce acqua e fertilizzanti sotto le radici, migliorando l’efficienza d’uso delle risorse e consentendo l’applicazione localizzata di biostimolanti. Secondo i dati riportati dall’azienda, rispetto ai metodi convenzionali le pratiche di agricoltura conservativa hanno evidenziato una riduzione del 50% delle emissioni di CO₂, un calo del 50-60% del consumo d’acqua e dell’inquinamento di aria e acqua, oltre a una riduzione del 90% della lisciviazione di nitrati in falda. Dal 2025, inoltre, le sperimentazioni su Underdrip sono state orientate anche all’efficienza nell’utilizzo dell’azoto, mentre l’ERSA, Ente Regionale per lo Sviluppo Agricolo, effettua campionamenti semestrali su qualità del suolo e biodiversità microbica.
Filiera controllata in crescita: oltre 108mila tonnellate di materie prime
Le pratiche sviluppate nei campi sperimentali ricadono poi sulla filiera agricola, che resta il centro del modello industriale di MartinoRossi. Nel 2025 le materie prime provenienti da filiera controllata sono salite a 108.858 tonnellate, contro le 86.466 tonnellate del 2024, con una crescita del 26%. In parallelo, gli approvvigionamenti esterni sono scesi del 18%, fermandosi a 23.542 tonnellate. È un dato che racconta una scelta precisa: più controllo diretto, meno dipendenza da canali esterni. E, di conseguenza, una tracciabilità più stretta.
A presidiare questo sistema è Campi d’Italia, business unit incaricata di coordinare oltre 700 partner agricoli su più di 16.000 ettari coltivati. L’obiettivo dichiarato è garantire materie prime di alta qualità, prive di allergeni e Ogm, attraverso controlli lungo l’intera catena del valore. Nel frattempo l’azienda ha proseguito il piano di sviluppo industriale avviato anche grazie al Pnrr, con interventi pensati per aumentare la capacità produttiva, migliorare l’efficienza dei processi e ridurre i consumi energetici. Una crescita, insomma, legata ai campi ma anche agli impianti.
Persone, occupazione e Piano 2030: più stabilità nel gruppo
Accanto a ricerca, filiera e investimenti, il bilancio dedica spazio alla dimensione interna dell’azienda. Nel 2025 l’organico di MartinoRossi è passato da 120 a 141 dipendenti, con un incremento del 17,5%, accompagnato dall’ingresso di nuove competenze e da un rafforzamento manageriale. La certificazione Great Place to Work, ottenuta con l’89% di partecipazione al sondaggio interno, ha registrato un punteggio finale superiore di 22 punti rispetto alla media nazionale. Un segnale, secondo l’azienda, del lavoro svolto su fiducia, rispetto e valorizzazione delle persone.
Il dato più concreto, però, riguarda la stabilizzazione: i contratti in somministrazione si sono ridotti del 68% rispetto al 2024. In una fase di espansione produttiva, non è un dettaglio secondario. Nella nota che accompagna il documento, MartinoRossi spiega che il Bilancio di Sostenibilità 2025 e il nuovo Piano 2030 confermano l’impegno a integrare obiettivi ambientali, sociali e industriali nella strategia di crescita, con target misurabili per i prossimi anni. La rotta, almeno sulla carta, è tracciata: meno impatti, più filiera controllata, più stabilità per chi lavora nel gruppo.

Concluse le analisi integrative sui campioni di vegetali a foglia larga prelevati attorno all’area dell’incendio: IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene sono presenti in concentrazioni molto basse e non costituiscono contaminazione ambientale. Trascurabile la presenza di metalli pesanti.

I risultati delle analisi concluse il 23 luglio 2026 integrano i dati di quelle concluse lo scorso 17 luglio e si riferiscono agli otto campioni di vegetali a foglia larga prelevati il 13 luglio a seguito dell’incendio all’azienda Spedi a Vecchiano (Pisa).
Nello specifico, i prelievi sono stati effettuati in sette punti considerati di massima ricaduta delle polveri e in un punto di “bianco”, situato in un’area non interessata dalla ricaduta.
Esito dei rilievi e inquinanti analizzati (vedi Rapporti di prova):

Diossine, Furani e PCB: come già comunicato, in nessuno degli otto campioni si registra la presenza di contaminazione da Diossine, Furani o PCB;
IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene: le ultime analisi concluse indicano la presenza di IPA e Benzo[a]Pirene, ma in concentrazioni estremamente basse e tali da non prefigurare un fenomeno di contaminazione ambientale;
Metalli pesanti: in base alla tipologia di materiale bruciato segnalata dalle autorità competenti, si è scelta l’estensione delle indagini anche ai metalli pesanti. Da queste analisi non sono emerse concentrazioni significative, fatta eccezione per Ferro, Alluminio e, in misura minore, Manganese. Trattandosi di elementi ubiquitari (naturalmente presenti nell’ambiente), la loro presenza non è necessariamente riconducibile alla ricaduta delle polveri dell’incendio.

Prosegue ancora la ricerca degli inquinanti riportati sopra, in campioni di filtri del PM10 di alcune stazioni di monitoraggio, tra le quali quella di Pisa Passi.

items.title: Acido picrico nei vecchi laboratori: a Brescia disinnescata una possibile tragedia
items.description: A Brescia, nei laboratori dismessi dell’ex Caffaro di via Francesco Nullo, durante le operazioni di bonifica del Sito di interesse nazionale, sono sta
items.body:
Ambiente

Acido picrico nei vecchi laboratori: a Brescia disinnescata una possibile tragedia

Redazione

-

24 Luglio 2026

Operatori specializzati ispezionano un laboratorio dismesso messo in sicurezza, con area transennata e presenza di soccorritori.

A Brescia, nei laboratori dismessi dell’ex Caffaro di via Francesco Nullo, durante le operazioni di bonifica del Sito di interesse nazionale, sono stati trovati nei giorni scorsi circa cinque chilogrammi di acido picrico secco e cristallizzato, una sostanza instabile che ha imposto lo stop immediato del cantiere per evitare rischi a tecnici e residenti. Il materiale, secondo quanto riferito dal CoGePir, il Consorzio Gestione Pirotecnici, era conservato in condizioni tali da renderlo sensibile a urti, vibrazioni, attrito e variazioni di temperatura.
Ex Caffaro, cantiere fermato dopo il ritrovamento dell’acido picrico
La segnalazione è partita dall’azienda impegnata nella messa in sicurezza dell’ex Caffaro, area industriale da anni al centro di interventi ambientali complessi. Dopo l’esame delle immagini inviate dal cantiere, il direttore generale del CoGePir, Piervittorio Trebucchi, ha chiesto di sospendere le lavorazioni, allontanare il personale e avvisare subito Vigili del Fuoco e artificieri. “Non bisognava muovere nulla”, avrebbe spiegato ai tecnici, secondo la ricostruzione del Consorzio. Solo allora l’area è stata isolata.
La Prefettura di Brescia, in base alle prime valutazioni, avrebbe preso in considerazione anche l’evacuazione di una zona con un raggio di circa un chilometro e mezzo. L’intervento degli specialisti ha poi permesso di neutralizzare il materiale, rimuoverlo e trasferirlo in un luogo idoneo, dove l’acido picrico cristallizzato è stato distrutto in condizioni controllate. Nessuno è rimasto ferito. Ma il caso, chiuso senza conseguenze, ha riaperto un tema meno visibile: la presenza di vecchie sostanze chimiche dimenticate in laboratori, scuole, ospedali e magazzini di ricerca.
Che cos’è l’acido picrico e perché diventa pericoloso
L’acido picrico, nome chimico 2,4,6-trinitrofenolo, è stato usato per anni nei laboratori di istologia, nell’industria dei coloranti e, in passato, anche come antisettico. Il suo impiego si è ridotto proprio per i problemi legati alla stabilità della sostanza. Di norma viene conservato umidificato o in soluzione acquosa; il rischio cresce quando l’acqua evapora e si formano cristalli anidri, di colore giallo, capaci di reagire con violenza a urti, calore o sfregamenti.Leggi ancheCiclone in arrivo, tensione alle stelle nei prossimi giorni: il meteo peggiora e si porta via tuttoParigi prevede la creazione di 500 nuove strade senza auto, destinate a diventare spazi verdi.
C’è poi un secondo elemento, non meno insidioso: il contatto con i metalli. L’acido picrico può formare picrati metallici, composti più sensibili, soprattutto in presenza di vecchi tappi, utensili o contenitori non compatibili. Per questo un flacone datato, magari con tappo bloccato o cristalli visibili sul collo, non deve essere aperto né spostato. Sembra un normale recipiente da laboratorio. Eppure, in quel momento, anche una vibrazione può diventare un problema serio.
Cosa fare davanti a un contenitore sospetto
Le indicazioni diffuse dal CoGePir sono nette: davanti a un possibile contenitore di acido picrico secco non bisogna improvvisare. Il recipiente non va toccato, mosso, aperto o fotografato da vicino; occorre allontanare le persone, impedire l’accesso al locale e chiamare immediatamente i Vigili del Fuoco e le autorità competenti. “Il tentativo di svitare un tappo può bastare”, ha spiegato il Consorzio, richiamando la necessità di lasciare ogni valutazione a personale formato.
La gestione di questi ritrovamenti richiede un coordinamento tra pubblica sicurezza, Vigili del Fuoco, responsabili delle bonifiche e operatori specializzati nel trattamento di materiali esplodenti. L’acido picrico essiccato, pur avendo caratteristiche esplosive, non coincide sempre con un ordigno dotato di innesco. Proprio per questo servono procedure chiare: stabilire se mettere in sicurezza il contenitore, rimuoverlo o procedere alla neutralizzazione sul posto è una decisione tecnica, non amministrativa né affidata al buon senso del momento.
Vecchi depositi da controllare, smaltimento solo con ditte autorizzate
Il caso di Brescia non sarebbe isolato. Secondo il CoGePir, vecchi flaconi di acido picrico possono ancora trovarsi in laboratori universitari, istituti scolastici, strutture sanitarie e magazzini di enti di ricerca. Nel maggio 2026, riferisce il Consorzio, una scuola di Genova sarebbe stata evacuata dopo il ritrovamento di una piccola quantità della sostanza nel laboratorio scientifico. La prevenzione, però, non significa aprire armadi e scatoloni senza criterio: servono inventari aggiornati, verifiche affidate a personale qualificato e procedure di emergenza già condivise.
Quando l’acido picrico è ancora utilizzato, deve essere conservato in contenitori compatibili, senza parti metalliche, mantenuto umido e controllato con regolarità. Lo smaltimento non può avvenire negli scarichi, nei normali rifiuti di laboratorio o tramite trasporto autonomo: occorrono imprese autorizzate alla gestione di rifiuti pericolosi con caratteristiche esplosive, nel rispetto delle norme ambientali e di pubblica sicurezza. Secondo i dati forniti dal Consorzio, nel 2025 il CoGePir ha raccolto e gestito oltre 51 mila chilogrammi di rifiuti pirotecnici, mentre nei primi sei mesi del 2026 ne sarebbero già stati trattati più di 40 mila. Numeri che raccontano un problema concreto: un flacone dimenticato per anni, in fondo a un armadio, può trasformarsi in una minaccia per lavoratori, cittadini e ambiente.

Per la rubrica “Dialoghi con l’autore e l’autrice” abbiamo intervistato Chiara Mezzalama, autrice di Dopo la pioggia

Dopo la pioggia, il romanzo di Chiara Mezzalama, affronta temi urgenti come il cambiamento climatico, cercando di coinvolgere le lettrici e i lettori non solo attraverso i numeri e i dati ma anche le emozioni. Ne abbiamo parlato con l’autrice in una caldissima giornata d’inizio estate, che è diventata spunto naturale per riflettere sulla crisi climatica e sulle sue conseguenze.
 
Nel romanzo emerge chiaramente l’idea che dati e statistiche, da soli, non bastino più a raccontare la crisi climatica. Perché?
Negli ultimi anni è cresciuta la sensibilità verso questi temi, ma continuiamo ad agire con troppa lentezza. Per questo credo che sia necessario parlare anche alle emozioni. La crisi climatica è sistemica, riguarda tutti noi e ha conseguenze imprevedibili persino per la nostra stessa esistenza sul pianeta.
 
In questo senso, quale può essere il ruolo della narrativa?
Il romanzo può diventare uno strumento prezioso perché, attraverso i personaggi, il lettore vive esperienze che potrebbero essere le sue. Non incontra semplicemente dati o notizie, spesso catastrofiche, ma persone nelle quali riconoscersi. È questo il potere della narrativa: creare empatia attraverso le storie e rendere concreta una realtà che spesso percepiamo come lontana o astratta ma che invece è molto vicina. Se riusciamo a coinvolgere lettrici e lettori sul piano emotivo, diventa più facile sviluppare una consapevolezza profonda e, di conseguenza, spirito critico e volontà di agire.
 
Nel libro gli effetti del cambiamento climatico – la siccità, il caldo estremo, le piogge violente – non producono solo danni materiali ma incidono profondamente anche sulla dimensione psicologica dei protagonisti. Pensa che oggi ci sia sufficiente consapevolezza di questo aspetto?
Si comincia a parlarne di più. Oggi conosciamo fenomeni come l’ecoansia, ma anche la solastalgia, cioè quel senso di angoscia e di perdita provocato dal deterioramento dell’ambiente in cui viviamo. Pensiamo a un ghiacciaio che abbiamo visto da bambini e che oggi non esiste più: non perdiamo soltanto un paesaggio, perdiamo anche una parte della nostra memoria e della nostra identità.
Ci siamo però anche incastrati in un unico modello di sviluppo che sembra concepire soltanto la crescita economica, senza riuscire a immaginare alternative. Ed è proprio qui che gli artisti possono dare un contributo fondamentale. La loro libertà creativa permette di mostrare prospettive nuove e inattese. Molti stanno affrontando il tema della crisi climatica attraverso le arti figurative, il cinema e la narrativa. È un segnale importante, che può trasformarsi in una spinta all’azione e aiutarci anche a superare gli stati d’ansia che questa inevitabilmente genera.
 
Cosa possiamo fare concretamente? Il singolo può davvero fare la differenza?
Le scelte individuali sono importanti e possono contribuire a contrastare il cambiamento climatico. Dobbiamo però essere consapevoli che, da sole, hanno un impatto limitato se non diventano anche scelte collettive. La vera forza nasce quando cresce uno spirito critico condiviso, capace di diffondere una cultura ecologista. È così che prendono forma richieste sempre più forti nei confronti della politica e delle istituzioni.
 
Nel romanzo c’è una giovanissima donna che incarna proprio questo spirito ecologista. Che ruolo possono avere oggi i movimenti ambientalisti? E i giovani sono davvero più sensibili delle altre generazioni?
I movimenti ecologisti hanno un ruolo fondamentale nello sviluppo del pensiero critico. Purtroppo, però, la politica sembra ancora non ascoltare le richieste che arrivano dalla società e questo crea uno scollamento profondo. Nei giovani esiste una consapevolezza molto forte della crisi climatica ma la classe politica e spesso anche i media non riescono a raccogliere questa energia e trasformarla in cambiamento.
Esistono moltissime persone impegnate concretamente nel contrasto agli effetti del cambiamento climatico purtroppo queste esperienze vengono raccontate come episodi isolati, mentre in realtà sono sempre più numerose. La politica sembra trovarsi spesso in una sorta di zona cieca, incapace di tradurre in azioni concrete le istanze della società.
 
Lei vive a Parigi. Il modello della “città dei quindici minuti” può rappresentare un’alternativa concreta?
Credo di sì. Parigi è cambiata molto negli ultimi anni, soprattutto dopo la pandemia. Sono stati fatti importanti investimenti sulla mobilità sostenibile: limitando il traffico si è ridotto l’inquinamento atmosferico e quello acustico e molte aree urbane sono state restituite ai cittadini come luoghi di incontro e di socializzazione sia per bambini che per adulti. È un esempio di come le richieste della società possano tradursi in politiche capaci di cambiare realmente il volto di una città.
 
Vorrei concludere parlando della protagonista del romanzo, Elena. È una donna che attraversa una profonda crisi personale e ritrova la propria identità anche grazie al contatto con la natura. A me è sembrata una figura portatrice di speranza. È una lettura che condivide?
Credo che le donne abbiano una straordinaria capacità di ricucire gli strappi. La gioia è una scelta e, proprio per questo, contiene in sé qualcosa di rivoluzionario e di resistente. Il contatto con la natura è fonte di gioia, così come lo sono le relazioni con gli altri, che ricostruiscono il tessuto sociale.
Le nostre scelte dovrebbero nascere dalla gioia. È una scelta profondamente politica, che si accompagna all’idea del dono, cioè alla possibilità di liberarci dalla logica del tornaconto personale. Questo ci apre a una diversa idea di libertà, nel modo in cui viviamo il tempo e nelle relazioni con gli altri. Questo è già un modo concreto di cambiare il mondo che ci circonda.
Dobbiamo prendere spunto dalla natura, che ci insegna un’altra logica: non è efficiente, almeno non nel senso in cui intendiamo oggi l’efficienza. Basta pensare al tempo necessario perché un albero cresca. Per questo abbiamo bisogno di una narrazione diversa, capace di aiutarci ad abitare il tempo che stiamo vivendo senza lasciarci trascinare verso la rovina ma aprendoci alla possibilità di immaginare un futuro differente.
